Apple has been ordered to respond by Monday to a complaint filed by Epic Games with Brazilian antitrust regulators. Epic alleges that Apple is interpreting its obligations under a recent App Store antitrust agreement in Brazil in a restrictive manner. Here's the details.

少少背景資料

Two months ago, Apple announced that it would now allow developers to distribute their apps through alternative app marketplaces in Brazil.

The change was part of a settlement agreement that ended a years-long antitrust investigation. That investigation stemmed from a complaint filed by Latin American e-commerce giant MercadoLibre over Apple's App Store rules.

Under the new terms, developers in Brazil can distribute iOS apps through alternative app marketplaces, with payment options outside of Apple's IAP system.

Apple also introduced a new commission structure, including a 5% "core technology fee" on digital goods and services sold through apps distributed outside of the App Store. For more details on the structure, click here.

Epic challenges Apple's implementation

According to a report today from Brazilian newspaper O Globo (relayed by MacMagazine), Epic recently filed a petition with Brazilian antitrust regulator CADE, alleging that Apple has placed "structural, technical, and access barriers" that undermine the practical viability of alternative app distribution.

Epic points out that, although the new Brazilian terms apply only to iOS apps, Apple's agreement with CADE "explicitly covers iPadOS."

Epic is also reportedly objecting to so-called "scare sheets," notices designed to discourage users from installing apps from outside the App Store. Epic is also challenging the existing installation flow, claiming that it requires nine steps, compared to the six-step process Apple uses in Europe.

According to O Globo, Epic further pointed out that Apple's original installation flow in Europe required 15 steps, but after being asked to reduce it to six, "download abandonment rates dropped from 65% to 25%."

Finally, Epic told CADE that Apple's reporting requirements go "far beyond what is necessary to calculate fees," allowing the company "to monitor competitors' business models."

O Globo says CADE has given Apple until Monday to respond. Apple has not publicly commented on the matter.
